D960.about: Schubert’s last piano sonata, composed weeks before his death, a vast, unhurried work of unusual length and serenity, its first movement famous for a distant, rumbling trill in the bass that interrupts the opening melody’s calm and returns throughout the movement like a distant premonition.
D960.ctx: Composed in September 1828, the last of a final trilogy of piano sonatas (D. 958, 959, 960) written in a remarkable creative surge just two months before Schubert’s death from typhoid fever at thirty-one; none of the three were published until a decade later, and all had to wait even longer for wide recognition.
parts: A long, unhurried movement built around a distant, ominous bass trill.
A deeply melancholy, hymn-like slow movement.
facts: The last of three piano sonatas Schubert composed in the final weeks of his life.
Not published until a decade after his death.
Its opening movement is marked by a distant, recurring bass trill.

D958.about: The first of Schubert’s final trio of piano sonatas, darker and more turbulent than its two companions, its opening theme bearing a resemblance to a theme by Beethoven, whose recent death in 1827 weighed heavily on Schubert as he composed this final group of works.
D958.ctx: Composed in September 1828, among the last works Schubert wrote before his death that November, part of a sonata trilogy that shows Schubert directly engaging with the example of Beethoven, whom he had idolized and whose funeral he had helped carry a torch at the year before.
facts: The first of Schubert’s final trilogy of piano sonatas, written weeks before his death.
Its opening theme has been linked to a theme of Beethoven.
Schubert had been a torchbearer at Beethoven’s funeral the previous year.

D894.about: Nicknamed the ’Fantasie’ sonata by its publisher, though it is a true four-movement sonata rather than a fantasy, distinguished by an unusually spacious, unhurried opening movement that Schumann described admiringly as the most perfect in form and conception of all Schubert’s works.
D894.ctx: Composed in 1826 and published the following year, one of the few Schubert piano sonatas to be published in his own lifetime, likely because its lyrical, unhurried character made it more immediately appealing to contemporary taste than some of his more expansive later sonatas.
parts: A spacious, songful opening movement Schumann praised as Schubert’s most perfectly formed.
facts: One of the few Schubert piano sonatas published during his own lifetime.
Schumann praised its opening movement as the most perfectly formed of all Schubert’s works.
Its publisher, not Schubert, gave it the ’Fantasie’ nickname.

D760.about: Nicknamed the ’Wanderer Fantasy’ for its use of a theme from Schubert’s own song ’Der Wanderer’ as the basis for a set of continuous variations spanning all four traditional sonata movements played without pause. One of the most technically demanding works in Schubert’s output, Schubert himself reportedly gave up partway through attempting to play it, exclaiming that the devil himself could play it.
D760.ctx: Composed in 1822, drawing on the melody of Schubert’s own 1816 song setting a poem about a lonely wanderer, the piece profoundly influenced Liszt, who admired its unified, single-movement structure so much that he later arranged it for piano and orchestra and modeled his own B minor Sonata’s continuous form partly on it.
parts: Allegro con fuoco ma non troppo
A bold opening movement built from the ’Wanderer’ theme’s rhythm.
A set of variations on the actual melody of ’Der Wanderer’.
A fugal finale bringing the cycle to a triumphant close.
facts: Based on a theme from Schubert’s own song ’Der Wanderer’.
Schubert reportedly found it too difficult to play himself.
Profoundly influenced Liszt’s own continuous, single-movement forms.

D899/3.about: The most popular of Schubert’s eight impromptus, a serene, flowing piece built on a broad, arpeggiated accompaniment beneath a simple, songlike melody, often compared in mood to a barcarolle for its gentle, rocking motion.
D899/3.ctx: Composed in 1827, the year before Schubert’s death, as the third of the Four Impromptus, D. 899, though the set was not published until decades after his death, and even then with the key of this particular piece altered by the publisher from Schubert’s original G-flat major to the more conventionally notated G major.
facts: The most frequently performed of Schubert’s eight impromptus.
Its publisher altered Schubert’s original key from G-flat to G major.
Not published until decades after Schubert’s death.

D935/2.about: A gently lyrical impromptu built on a warm, flowing melody framing a more agitated central section, the second of the second set of Four Impromptus that some scholars believe Schubert conceived as a disguised four-movement piano sonata.
D935/2.ctx: Composed in 1827, alongside the first set of impromptus, D. 899, this second set was not published until 1839, over a decade after Schubert’s death, and its four pieces’ contrasting keys and characters have led some scholars to suggest Schubert intended them as a unified sonata-like cycle.
facts: Some scholars believe the four impromptus of D. 935 were conceived as a disguised sonata.
Not published until 1839, over a decade after Schubert’s death.
Composed the same year as the first set of impromptus, D. 899.

D780/3.about: Nicknamed ’Air russe’ though the connection to Russian music is likely spurious, the third and by far most famous of Schubert’s six Moments musicaux, a brief, insistently rhythmic piece whose obsessive dotted rhythm gives it an unmistakably folk-dance character.
D780/3.ctx: Composed over several years between 1823 and 1828 and published together as the set of six Moments musicaux, D. 780, this particular piece had actually been published separately several years earlier under a different title before being incorporated into the completed set.
facts: By far the most famous of Schubert’s six Moments musicaux.
Its nickname, ’Air russe’, is likely a later, unfounded addition.
Had been published separately years before the complete set appeared.

D667.about: Nicknamed the ’Trout’ Quintet for its fourth movement, a set of variations on Schubert’s own song ’Die Forelle’ (’The Trout’). Unusually scored, replacing the standard piano quintet’s second violin with a double bass, giving the ensemble an especially warm, resonant bass register.
D667.ctx: Composed in 1819 during a happy summer holiday in the Austrian town of Steyr, commissioned by the amateur cellist and music patron Sylvester Paumgartner, who specifically requested that Schubert include a set of variations on his already-popular song about a trout.
parts: Variations on Schubert’s own song ’Die Forelle’.
D667.sc: Piano, violin, viola, cello, double bass
facts: Its nickname comes from variations on Schubert’s own song about a trout.
Uses a double bass in place of the usual second violin, an unusual scoring for a piano quintet.
Commissioned by an amateur cellist during a holiday in Steyr.

D810.about: Nicknamed ’Death and the Maiden’ for its second movement, a set of variations on Schubert’s own earlier song of the same name, in which Death gently persuades a frightened young woman to come with him. One of the darkest and most emotionally searing works in the string quartet repertoire, composed while Schubert, aware he was seriously ill, was confronting his own mortality.
D810.ctx: Composed in 1824, not long after Schubert had learned he was suffering from what was likely syphilis, a diagnosis that profoundly darkened his outlook; he wrote to a friend around this time that he felt himself ’the most unhappy and wretched creature in the world’.
parts: Variations on Schubert’s song ’Der Tod und das Mädchen’.
facts: Its second movement varies Schubert’s own song ’Der Tod und das Mädchen’.
Composed shortly after Schubert learned of his own serious illness.
Considered one of the darkest works in the string quartet repertoire.

D703.about: Nicknamed ’Quartettsatz’ (’quartet movement’), a single, turbulent completed movement of a string quartet Schubert abandoned after sketching only a fragment of a second; despite its incompleteness, the finished movement is regarded as one of Schubert’s finest chamber works, restless and harmonically adventurous.
D703.ctx: Composed in December 1820, at a transitional point in Schubert’s development as a chamber composer, the fragment was left unpublished and largely unknown until decades after his death, when it was recognized as an important bridge between his earlier, more conventional quartets and his mature late works.
facts: A single completed movement; Schubert abandoned the quartet after sketching a second.
Not published until decades after his death.
Regarded as a key transitional work in Schubert’s development as a chamber composer.

D759.about: Nicknamed the ’Unfinished’ Symphony, consisting of only two completed movements rather than the usual four; Schubert left the manuscript with a friend and it was not performed until decades after his death. Despite, or perhaps because of, its incompleteness, it has become one of the most beloved symphonies ever written.
D759.ctx: Composed in 1822 but abandoned after two movements for reasons that remain unclear — theories range from illness to simple loss of interest — the manuscript sat forgotten for over forty years until the conductor Johann Herbeck rediscovered it and gave its belated premiere in 1865.
parts: A serene, richly melodic slow movement.
facts: Consists of only two completed movements.
Not performed until 1865, decades after Schubert’s death.
One of the most popular symphonies in the repertoire despite its incompleteness.

D944.about: Nicknamed ’The Great’ to distinguish it from Schubert’s earlier, shorter Sixth Symphony (also in C major), an expansive, symphonically ambitious work of unprecedented length for its time, famously championed and premiered after Schubert’s death by Robert Schumann, who discovered the manuscript gathering dust at the home of Schubert’s brother.
D944.ctx: Composed in 1825–26 but never performed in Schubert’s lifetime, the symphony sat unknown until Schumann, visiting Vienna in 1838, found the manuscript and arranged for its belated premiere under Mendelssohn’s direction in Leipzig the following year, praising its ’heavenly length’.
parts: A spacious introduction leading to an expansive main movement.
facts: Discovered by Robert Schumann a decade after Schubert’s death.
Premiered under Mendelssohn’s direction in Leipzig in 1839.
Schumann famously praised its ’heavenly length’.

D328.about: A dramatic setting of Goethe’s ballad about a father riding through the night with his sick child, who is pursued and finally claimed by the supernatural Erlking; Schubert’s setting, composed when he was just eighteen, uses relentless triplet figuration to suggest the galloping horse and distinct vocal characterizations for narrator, father, son and the Erlking himself, all sung by a single performer.
D328.ctx: Composed in 1815 in a single sitting, according to the well-known but possibly embellished account of Schubert’s friends, the song became one of his most celebrated works and helped establish his reputation, even though, like much of his early output, it was initially rejected by the publisher Breitkopf & Härtel.
facts: Composed when Schubert was just eighteen.
A single singer voices four distinct characters: narrator, father, son and the Erlking.
Initially rejected by the publisher Breitkopf & Härtel.

D839.about: Widely known simply as Schubert’s ’Ave Maria’, though it originally set different words entirely — a prayer from Walter Scott’s poem The Lady of the Lake, sung by the character Ellen. The Latin ’Ave Maria’ text now usually heard was fitted to Schubert’s melody only later, by other hands, and does not match his original setting word for word.
D839.ctx: Composed in 1825 as part of a set of seven songs from Scott’s Lady of the Lake, translated into German, this piece — Ellen’s third song, a prayer to the Virgin Mary within the story — became so beloved that it was eventually detached from its original context and is now known almost universally by its opening words, ’Ave Maria’.
facts: Originally set a German translation of a prayer from Walter Scott’s The Lady of the Lake, not the Latin Ave Maria text.
The now-familiar Latin words were fitted to the melody later, by other hands.
One of Schubert’s most widely recognized melodies.
